title: Web App Vulnerabilities Concept Map
subtitle: The ten vulnerability classes you actually meet in the wild. Tap a bubble.
searchPlaceholder: Search: e.g. XSS, CSRF, SSTI, LFI…
rootDesc: Where the OWASP Top 10 names root-cause risk categories, this map covers the concrete vulnerability classes — the actual bugs found in tests and exploited in incidents. Each one maps back to an OWASP category and a CWE, and each has a detection angle a SOC can watch for in WAF and application logs. The last module covers how to read an advisory when one lands.

modules.title: SQL Injection
modules.desc: Input reaches a database query unparameterized, so the attacker's text is parsed as SQL. Low frequency today but high impact: authentication bypass, full table dumps, sometimes code execution on the database host.

children.title: Union-based
children.desc: Appending a UNION SELECT to pull data from other tables into the visible response.

children.title: Blind / boolean
children.desc: No data is returned, so the attacker infers it one bit at a time from how the page responds to true/false conditions.

children.title: Time-based
children.desc: Same inference, but using deliberate delays as the signal when even the page content gives nothing away.

children.title: Detection
children.desc: SQL keywords and quote characters in parameters, sudden spikes in 500 errors, or many near-identical requests differing by one character.

children.title: Defense
children.desc: Parameterized queries everywhere; least-privilege database accounts; never build a query by string concatenation.

modules.title: Cross-Site Scripting
modules.desc: Attacker-controlled script executes in another user's browser under the application's origin. High frequency, and the usual payoff is session theft or actions performed as the victim.

children.title: Stored
children.desc: The payload is saved server-side (a comment, a profile field) and fires for every user who views it. The most damaging variant.

children.title: Reflected
children.desc: The payload rides in the request and comes straight back in the response — needs the victim to click a crafted link.

children.title: DOM-based
children.desc: Never touches the server; client-side JavaScript writes untrusted input into the DOM unsafely.

children.title: Detection
children.desc: Script tags and event handlers in parameters, unusual outbound requests carrying cookie values.

children.title: Defense
children.desc: Context-aware output encoding, a strict Content-Security-Policy, and HttpOnly cookies so script cannot read the session.

modules.title: IDOR / Broken Object Access
modules.desc: An object reference — an id, filename, or account number — is accepted without checking that this user may access it. Trivial to exploit, and the single most common serious finding in API testing.

children.title: Sequential IDs
children.desc: Incrementing a numeric id in a URL and walking through other users' records one by one.

children.title: Mass assignment
children.desc: Sending extra fields (role, isAdmin, balance) that the server binds to the object without filtering.

children.title: Detection
children.desc: One session enumerating many distinct object ids in a short window — a pattern that stands out clearly in application logs.

children.title: Defense
children.desc: Check ownership server-side on every object access; prefer unguessable identifiers, but never rely on them as the control.

modules.title: Server-Side Request Forgery
modules.desc: The application fetches a URL supplied by the user, so the attacker makes the server issue requests on their behalf — from inside the network perimeter. Folded into Broken Access Control in the 2025 Top 10.

children.title: Cloud metadata access
children.desc: Pointing the server at its own cloud metadata endpoint to steal instance credentials and IAM tokens.

children.title: Internal port scanning
children.desc: Using response timing and error differences to map services that are not reachable from outside.

children.title: Detection
children.desc: Outbound requests from an application server to internal ranges or metadata addresses it has no business reaching.

children.title: Defense
children.desc: Allow-list destinations, block link-local and internal ranges at egress, and require authentication on internal services.

modules.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery
modules.desc: A victim's browser is tricked into sending an authenticated state-changing request to an application where they are already logged in — the request is genuine, the intent is not.

children.title: Forced state change
children.desc: A password change, transfer, or settings update fired from an attacker's page using the victim's live session.

children.title: Defense
children.desc: Anti-CSRF tokens tied to the session, SameSite cookie attributes, and re-authentication for high-value actions.

modules.title: Authentication Bypass
modules.desc: Reaching an authenticated context without valid credentials — through a flawed token, a skipped step, or a logic hole in the login flow.

children.title: JWT tampering
children.desc: Changing the algorithm to 'none' or exploiting a server that decodes a token without verifying its signature.

children.title: Session fixation
children.desc: Forcing a known session identifier on the victim before login, then reusing it afterward.

children.title: Forced browsing
children.desc: Navigating straight to a post-login URL that was only ever hidden, never protected.

children.title: Detection
children.desc: Successful access with malformed or unsigned tokens; sessions used from two distant locations at once.

modules.title: Insecure File Upload
modules.desc: An upload feature accepts a file it shouldn't, or stores it somewhere it can be executed. The shortest path from a web bug to code running on the server.

children.title: Web shell upload
children.desc: Uploading a script file into a web-served directory and then requesting it, giving command execution.

children.title: Content-type spoofing
children.desc: Faking the declared type or extension to get past a check that trusts what the client claims.

children.title: Defense
children.desc: Validate by content not extension, store outside the web root, rename on save, and serve downloads through a handler.

modules.title: Path Traversal / LFI
modules.desc: A file path built from user input escapes its intended directory, letting an attacker read — and sometimes include and execute — files elsewhere on the host.

children.title: Directory traversal
children.desc: Sequences like ../ walking up out of the intended folder to reach configuration files, keys, or password files.

children.title: Local File Inclusion
children.desc: The traversed file is not just read but included and interpreted, which can escalate to code execution.

children.title: Detection
children.desc: Traversal sequences or encoded variants in path parameters; application reads of files far outside its own tree.

modules.title: SSTI & Deserialization
modules.desc: Two different bugs with the same ending: untrusted input is handed to something that evaluates it, and the attacker gets code execution on the server.

children.title: Server-Side Template Injection
children.desc: User input placed into a template that is then rendered, so template syntax in the input is evaluated.

children.title: Insecure deserialization
children.desc: Serialized objects from an untrusted source are reconstructed, triggering gadget chains that run attacker code.

children.title: Defense
children.desc: Never render user input as a template; accept only signed or schema-validated serialized data, or use plain data formats instead.

modules.title: Exposed Config & Secrets
modules.desc: Nothing is injected and nothing is bypassed — the information was simply left reachable. Consistently among the first things an attacker checks, and among the easiest to fix.

children.title: Exposed .git / backups
children.desc: Source repositories, database dumps, or editor backup files left served by the web server.

children.title: Leaked API keys
children.desc: Secrets in client-side JavaScript, public repositories, or error output.

children.title: Open admin panels
children.desc: Management interfaces reachable from the internet, often still on default credentials.

children.title: Detection
children.desc: Requests probing for well-known sensitive paths — a steady background pattern in any internet-facing web log.

modules.title: HTTP Request Smuggling
modules.desc: Two servers in a chain — a proxy, load balancer, or WAF in front and the application server behind — disagree on where one HTTP request ends and the next begins. The attacker exploits that disagreement to smuggle a second request past the front-end's checks. Exactly the flaw behind CVE-2026-88773 in the Citrix NetScaler bulletin.

children.title: CL.TE / TE.CL
children.desc: The classic variants: one server trusts the Content-Length header, the other trusts Transfer-Encoding. The mismatch leaves part of the attacker's body sitting at the front of the next request.

children.title: Front-end control bypass
children.desc: The smuggled request never passes the front-end's authentication, routing, or WAF rules — it is already inside when the back-end parses it.

children.title: Request poisoning
children.desc: The smuggled fragment prepends onto another user's request, so a victim receives the attacker's response or performs an action they never made.

children.title: Where it appears
children.desc: Anywhere there is a proxy chain — CDNs, reverse proxies, and edge appliances like NetScaler that terminate and re-issue HTTP.

children.title: Defense
children.desc: Normalize requests at the edge, reject those carrying both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding, and use HTTP/2 end to end where possible.

modules.title: Reading CVEs
modules.desc: How to judge whether an advisory is an emergency or a Monday task. The score alone rarely tells you; the vector and the preconditions do.

children.title: CVE vs CWE
children.desc: A CVE is one specific vulnerability in one product. A CWE is the weakness class it belongs to — and OWASP categories are built out of CWEs, which is how an advisory maps back to what you already know.

children.title: CVSS vector
children.desc: Read the vector, not just the number. AV:N means reachable over the network, AC:L means easy, PR:N means no credentials needed, UI:N means no victim action required. All four together is the worst case.

children.title: Preconditions
children.desc: A high score with a narrow precondition may not touch you at all; a slightly lower score that applies to the default configuration probably does. Always check which of your appliances actually meet the condition.

children.title: CISA KEV
children.desc: The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — a CVE listed there is confirmed exploited in the wild, which outranks any score when deciding what to patch first.

children.title: Patch is not enough
children.desc: If an internet-facing device was exploited before the fix, the attacker may already have a webshell, stolen session, or persistence. Patching closes the door; it does not evict anyone already inside.
